title: Nerves and your own zone
summary: Nerves before a competition are normal. How to find the level that suits you, read a racing heart as readiness, and know when to ask for help.

body.html: Your first Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting competition is likely to make you nervous: new people, a referee, a score sheet, spectators. That is normal. Experienced shooters feel nerves too; they have learned to work with them.

When you are nervous, your body releases adrenaline. The heart beats faster, breathing gets shallow and the hands may shake. Some shooters then rush the gun mount, stop the gun or lift the head to see the break.
There is no single right level of nerves. Research suggests each athlete has a personal zone: some shoot well a little wound up, others when calm.
To find your zone, rate how wound up you felt from 0 to 10 after each round, and note your score. After a few weeks you may start to see which level suits you.

Across many studies, athletes who worried did only slightly worse, while athletes who felt confident did clearly better. Confidence grows from preparation: a routine you trust and targets you have trained. None of these studies is from clay shooting, so most likely this works the same way in Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting.

A racing heart can also be read as readiness. Telling yourself “I'm ready, this is energy” instead of trying to calm down helped in several studies outside sport. In them, people had to perform under pressure, for example by speaking in front of others.

Tell yourself what to do, not what to avoid: “see the target” rather than “just don't miss”. More in Cue words and self-talk. Slow breathing before the stand can also help: see Breathing: what to do and when.

Preparation removes surprises. Arrive early, know your start time and layout, and check your cartridges, glasses and ear protection the evening before. More in Competition day: sleep, coffee, water and food.

After a miss, do not argue with yourself in public. Throwing the gun, or aggression or violence towards the referee or other shooters, counts as loss of self-control; Sporting™ also names abusive language. The referee reports it to the jury, which can expel the shooter (Chapter 8 · Loss of self-control, Chapter 21 · Loss of self-control). Breathe out and think of the next target: see Reset after a miss.
Start with club shoots: the atmosphere is calmer, and you learn the procedure with less pressure. With each competition, nerves become more familiar.
If nerves stay strong for weeks, spoil your sleep or mood, or keep you away from shooting, talk to a sport psychologist or a doctor. That is a normal step, like seeing a coach for technique.

Do not take anything to calm your nerves without a doctor. Under the WADA list, beta-blockers are prohibited at all times in shooting, even on prescription, unless you have a TUE, an official medical exemption. Treat them as prohibited in Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting too: see Medicines and anti-doping: beta-blockers, TUE, supplements.

notes.html: Before your child's competition, keep the morning calm and the talk about ordinary things. Do not ask about the score you expect.

key_points.html: Nerves are normal; the level that suits you is personal.
Rate how wound up you feel from 0 to 10 after rounds to find your zone.
Tell yourself what to do, not what to avoid.
After a miss: breathe out and go to the next target; losing self-control breaks the rules.
Strong nerves for weeks: talk to a sport psychologist or a doctor.

did_you_know.html: A little nervousness is normal and helps many shooters focus. The useful level differs from person to person, which is why it is worth finding your own.

quiz.q: What does research say about the right level of nerves?

options.text: It differs from shooter to shooter
The calmer you are, the better you shoot
Five out of ten suits all shooters

quiz.explain: Research suggests personal zones: some shoot well a little wound up, others when calm.

quiz.q: Which self-talk cue is more helpful?
quiz.explain: A cue that describes the action you want tends to help more than one about what to avoid.

quiz.q: What can happen if a shooter throws the gun down or turns aggressive towards the referee?

options.text: The target is simply shot again
The jury can expel the shooter

quiz.explain: Loss of self-control is reported to the jury, which can expel the shooter at once, in both disciplines.
